article_text:
The raw heartache of high school’s final days, in all their promise and messiness, becomes the ground for an immersive, ethnographically precise exploration of teenage feelings in “ La Gradiva .”

Written, helmed, and shot by Marine Atlan , the French-language coming-of-age story is set in and around Naples and Pompeii on a class trip that proves profoundly life-shifting for all — and with a terrific cast of first-time actors she found literally on the street, all encouraged to bring their own perspectives to the material. Atlan’s first as a director, the film won Cannes Critics’ Week, where the smarthouse indie outfit 1-2 Special bought it for a winter stateside release.

Launched in 2025, 1-2 Special also held court at the New York Film Festival (NYFF) with Cannes-winning German Oscar entry “ Everytime ” and bought Venice Prize winner and NYFF breakout “ A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra ” earlier this week. The films form a trio of emotional studies of adolescence shaped by grief. While “Everytime” heads for a qualifying run in November ahead of wider release, “ La Gradiva ” is first up for theaters, launching on December 18. For cinephiles, these were among NYFF’s buzziest discoveries.

France ultimately chose the Russian-language (and partly French-produced) “Minotaur” to represent in the Best International Feature Oscar category, but “La Gradiva” is riding high as one of the year’s most acclaimed films. Especially after outstanding play in Toronto and New York. Atlan, in her mid-30s, has long worked as a cinematographer, building toward the directorial debut she shot herself — announcing a multihyphenate talent who will surely graduate to the next level at Cannes with her next film. Critics’ Week has historically helped propel now-renowned filmmakers like Bernardo Bertolucci, Andrea Arnold, Leos Carax, Julia Ducournau, Alejandro González Iñárritu, David Robert Mitchell, Justine Triet, François Ozon, and Gaspar Noé to competition and onto the international scene. Atlan’s arrival heralds a discovery on their level.

A loose-limbed vérité drama whose dialogue and scenarios grew from Atlan’s screenplay, co-written with Anne Brouillet, and the actors’ improvisation during rehearsal, “La Gradiva” opens both a window onto teen desire and yearning, and something much grander and sprawling. It follows a troupe of French teenagers as they travel to Naples, guided by their overworked teacher, Mercier (Antonia Buresi), who wants to show her students another slice of the world before they enter adulthood.

There’s the drifting, haunted, intense-eyed Toni (Colas Quignard), who seizes the trip to explore his sexuality — especially with one delicately directed Grindr hookup — even as he harbors a crush on his best friend, the charismatic James (Mitia Capellier-Audat). We first meet James, the most politically activated of the bunch, having sex (perhaps for the first time?) with a female classmate on the train as Toni watches, glowering. This voyeuristic moment sets the stage for painful revelations to follow, as “La Gradiva” gradually mines the fissures of a friendship.

Meanwhile, the bookish, introverted, aspiring artist Suzanne (Suzanne Gerin) has, in her own words, deemed herself “unfuckable,” but she will have a sensual awakening — and more — of her own. They immerse themselves in art history and archeology, and in Toni’s own fraught family history tied to the place, as they discover the ruins of Pompeii and bodies desiccated under ash many, many centuries ago. All the actors are what you’d call “nonprofessional.” But nothing about their deeply internalized performances feels nonprofessional, as they suffuse “La Gradiva” with a docudrama atmosphere. “I wasn’t against the idea of using actresses and actors who were professionals, even for the young people in the film, but it was very important to me that the actors and actresses be the same age as the characters,” Atlan told IndieWire, via translator Nicholas Elliott, during a recent IndieWire interview, speaking on the film’s two-year-long audition process.

“It’s relatively rare to find professionals of that young age. We did see some people who had acted before, did some casting sessions. What was really important for me was to have this sensation of realism, of something familiar, so that when people saw this film, they would be able to reconfigure faces that perhaps they knew from their own classes at school,” she said. “Having unknown faces would help produce that effect. So what happened is that my casting director, Julie Sokolowski, and I did what indeed we call street casting.”

That meant standing outside schools as kids left for the day, observing amateur theater groups, and attending political demonstrations in Paris. That’s how, for one, they discovered Mitia Capellier-Audat, who’d been participating in the city’s annual May 1 anarchist demonstration.

“We spent at least six months in the audition process with him because, in his case, it was really shifting the character quite significantly, really going towards something rather gender fluid,” Atlan said. “I did want some androgyny in the case of that character, but Mitia really has a femininity. So for that character, it was really quite a significant change.”

The actor is also “very politicized in his life,” so Atlan’s production had to respond, including in a pivotal scene where the students debate their own generation’s political positions. Some of the film’s situations emerged out of rehearsal improv. “When I saw Mitia make his arguments, when I saw him give his opinions, when I saw that he had a dialectic relationship to politics, I thought that this would be a very interesting thing to have the character have in that scene.”

Elsewhere, “in terms of Colas, he had been a dancer for 10 years,” Atlan said. “So when I was directing him as an actor, I really worked on his relationship to the body. Suzanne’s kind of rebellious temperament brought a lucidity to that character. So I would say that the actors’ personalities reinforced and deepened the interpretation or embodiment of the characters.”

The film took three years from start to finish. Building scenarios out of rehearsal “allowed us to constantly readapt or readjust the writing,” said Atlan, who also worked as a director of photography on other projects during pre-production.

“La Gradiva” proved demanding for the first-time actors because of the onscreen sensuality, and Atlan and her team had to adjust the level of intimacy required with their collaboration.

“I wanted this film to be about desire, to have that be an important theme of the film, but it was even more important to find the right actors and actresses to play the characters. So once we had our three leads, we had an intimacy coordinator, and we set up a situation where we worked with them to get them to the point where they were comfortable touching each other and so on,” she said. “They also gave me an official document listing what they were willing to do and what they weren’t willing to do. So to be very concrete, Colas did not want to kiss anyone. That, in some cases, meant that I had to rewrite things.”

But that reconfiguration also influenced how Atlan would film scenes. “When Toni meets an Italian man on Grindr, so much takes place off-scene, offscreen… I always had in mind that these are 17-year-olds, and it was unthinkable to try to make them do something they didn’t want to do.”

She was, after all, not making a Larry Clark movie (“we can’t do that,” Atlan laughed). But to that point, “La Gradiva” feels like the most immersive teen drama since the 1995 drug-and-sex-filled, New York-set “Kids” (a far cry from “La Gradiva” in that sense) reinvented the genre for independent film and delivered an ensemble of major new young actors.

As for what Atlan is up to next, “I just finished shooting a first feature by a woman director this summer as a director of photography. And now, little by little, I’m going to try to start writing my next feature film as I’m accompanying the release of [‘La Gradiva’]. I’m always going to try to keep that balance.”

“La Gradiva” opens from 1-2 Special stateside starting December 18.
excerpt_original: Coming-of-age and shattered innocence collide in this fall's Cannes Critics' Week winner from 1-2 Special. Writer/director/cinematographer Marine Atlan walks IndieWire through street-casting a Pompeii-set high-school drama for the ages.

‘Street Fighter’ is box office top dog

Paramount’s Street Fighter tops the worldwide box office for the October 16-18 weekend session with an estimated $51.2m – the lowest chart-topping number since mid-September, when Practical Magic 2 achieved this feat with a middling $46.0m debut.

So far, North America ($31.0m) is running ahead of international ($20.1m) for Street Fighter , which is presented by Paramount Pictures and Legendary Pictures in association with videogame company Capcom. Imax delivered $7.7m of the $51.2m opening total.

UK/Ireland leads international markets with an estimated $3.3m, ahead of Mexico ($1.8m), Australia ($1.6m), Brazil ($1.2m), France ($1.1m), Japan ($875,000) and Germany ($850,000).

Directed by Kitao Sakurai, the film boasts an eclectic ensemble cast combining the likes of Noah Centineo, Jason Momoa and rapper Curtis ’50 Cent’ Jackson with martial artist Andrew Koji and WWE wrestlers Cody Rhodes and Joe ’Roman Reigns’ Anoa’i.

The Street Fighter videogame series was earlier notably adapted for the big screen in 1994, with a Universal Pictures film starring Jean-Claude Van Damme. Box office reached $99.4m worldwide, according to available data. (Comparisons in this report are not adjusted for inflation.)

Production budget for this new Street Fighter film is reported at $82m. Given revenue splits with cinemas and marketing costs, the film has a fair way to go to achieve profitability – but the budget below $100m at least gives the autumn tentpole a fighting chance of doing so.

‘Jailer 2’ is close behind with $44m launch

Street Fighter tops the worldwide box office ahead of Indian film Jailer 2 , which lands in second place with an estimated $31.2m from 20 markets for the weekend period, and $44.5m since release last Thursday (October 15). North America contributes $5.3m of this total.

Nelson Dilipkumar’s Tamil-language action comedy is a sequel to his 2023 film Jailer , starring Rajinikanth in the title role. Lifetime box office for Jailer has been estimated at $73m.

‘Whalefall’ swims to $17.5m debut

Source: Walt Disney Studios

‘Whalefall’

Disney’s Whalefall enters the worldwide weekend chart in sixth place with an estimated $17.5m – just below a trio of holdover titles, Resident Evil , Other Mommy and Verity . Brian Duffield’s survival thriller saw international markets ($9.5m) edge ahead of North America ($8.0m).

The 20th Century Studios release stars Resident Evil ’s Austin Abrams as a young man trapped inside a sperm whale, and is adapted from Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel. The producer roster includes Brian Grazer for Imagine Entertainment.

Among international markets, Whalefall performed best in Mexico (an estimated $800,000), with UK/Ireland and China tied on $700,000, and France, Japan and Germany estimated at $500,000. Production budget is reported at $60m.

Among the holdover titles above Whalefall in the chart, Sony’s Resident Evil has now reached $361.2m – pulling convincingly ahead of the franchise’s previous best result (2016’s Resident Evil: The Final Chapter with $312.2m).

Amazon MGM Studios’ Verity has reached $145.3m worldwide – well ahead of the lifetime cumulative totals for previous Colleen Hoover adaptations Regretting You ($90.5m) and Reminders Of Him ($89.3m), but behind It Ends With Us ($351.4m).

‘Sense And Sensibility’ enters top 10 chart

Universal Picture/Focus Features’ Sense And Sensibility has entered the worldwide weekend top 10 chart for the first time, buoyed by release in North America (an estimated $7.25m opening). Worldwide total is now $18.5m.

Georgia Oakley’s Jane Austen adaptation expanded its footprint to 23 markets at the weekend, also opening in Australia (an estimated $781,000), Netherlands ($358,000), Germany ($291,000) and 12 other territories.

In cumulative, UK/Ireland leads with $7.7m after four weeks of release. France has reached $1.0m.

Future key markets include both Italy and Spain this coming week, with South Korea, Brazil and Mexico all later this month.

In 2020, Focus Features’ Austen adaptation Emma achieved a Covid-impacted $16.3m worldwide over its lifetime. In 2005, Focus Features’ Pride & Prejudice reached $131.9m worldwide. In 1995, Sony’s Sense And Sensibility (directed by Ang Lee) achieved $134.8m.

‘You Can See Everything’ crashes box office party with North America release

A24 documentary You Can See Everything lands in seventh place in the worldwide weekend listing from release solely in North America – with an estimated $15.0m. It’s the biggest documentary debut in the market since 2004’s Fahrenheit 9/11 , not counting concert films.

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything tracks the final days of freedom for disgraced Theranos co-founder Elizabeth Holmes, before she delivered herself to begin an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

Global rollout for the film will follow. The UK/Ireland release is set for November 20 via A24.

Making way for this week’s four new entries in the top 10 chart are a quartet of titles falling out of the listing: Warner Bros’ Digger , Sony’s The Social Reckoning , Universal/DreamWorks’ Forgotten Island and Indian crime thriller Drishyam: The Conclusion .

Forgotten Island added an estimated $5.6m worldwide at the weekend, taking the total to $60.3m. Among new openers, UK/Ireland leads with $1.7m. In cumulative, top international markets are Australia ($5.0m) and Philippines ($3.9m). Latter territory is the where the film is set. The global rollout is ongoing.

article_text:
Die Art Basel Paris schließt zwei Tage früher als geplant, um neuen Protesten in der Stadt zu entgehen. Die Kunstwelt, die immer auch ein wenig von Selbstbetrug lebt, wird schmerzhaft auf den Boden der Tatsachen geholt

Die Haufen verbrannter E-Bikes rauchten noch auf dem Asphalt im Marais, als die ersten Sammlerinnen und Sammler am vergangenen Wochenende für die Art Basel Paris anreisten. Straßen und Bürgersteige waren voller Glasscherben, Ladenbesitzer installierten Sperrholzplatten vor den zersplitterten Scheiben. Nicht nur Dior, Lacoste und Co., auch der Bäcker nebenan war Ziel der Attacken geworden. Und wer schon am Wochenende dagewesen war, hatte auch ausgiebig Tränengas eingeatmet, so erzählte es der Künstler Ingar Dragset , der gemeinsam mit seinem Kunstpartner Michael Elmgreen eine Ausstellung bei der Galerie Max Hetzler aufgebaut hatte.

Die Art Basel Paris reagierte mit verstärkten Sicherheitsmaßnahmen, mehr Absperrungen vor dem Grand Palais und mehr Kontrollen – und eröffnete doch wie geplant. Es war, nach den üblichen Kriterien, eine schöne Messe. Unten die soliden Blue Chips, darunter ein sagenhafter Modigliani für 100 Millionen Dollar. Oben die jüngeren Galerien, spannende Künstlerinnen und Künstler, Präsentationen voller Herzblut.

Karim Crippa , der neue Messechef, konnte stolz auf seine erste Show sein – und die Verkäufe während der VIP-Tage liefen dem Vernehmen nach gut. Offenbar ließen sich nur wenige Sammlerinnen und Sammler von den brutalen Bildern der Pariser Demonstrationen abhalten. Auf der Messe waren diese zwar immer wieder Thema des Smalltalks, aber eigentlich ging es ums Business und, wenn es gut lief, auch um Kunst.

Kann man die Skulptur als Wurfgeschoss verwenden?

Trotzdem blieb ein Unbehagen. Die zur Säule aufgetürmten Steinkugeln von Alicja Kwades Skulptur vor dem Grand Palais: Kann man die eigentlich als überdimensionale Wurfgeschosse verwenden? Und was ist, mon dieu , mit dem Glasdach des Grand Palais?

Das ungute Gefühl in dieser Messewoche rührte nicht nur von der Angst um die Kunst oder der Sorge her, nach dem Messebesuch von einer Demonstration eingekesselt zu werden. Es mischte sich auch mit dem unangenehmen Eindruck, plötzlich selbst zur Zielscheibe zu werden – als Teil eines Systems, das von genau jenem ungerechten Reichtum lebt, gegen den sich die sozialen Bewegungen wenden.

Das Kapital, das man braucht, um Kunst im oberen Segment zu sammeln, fällt eben nicht vom Himmel, sondern ist das Ergebnis einer Verteilung von Ressourcen, die allen Statistiken und Untersuchungen zufolge immer stärker zugunsten des obersten Prozents ausfällt. Auch in der Kunst schreitet die Konzentration von Geld und Macht an der Spitze des Betriebs voran, während die Mitte geschwächt wird. Und plötzlich, wenn nebenan die Barrikaden rauchen, wird es schwer, das zu vergessen.

"Sollen sie doch Kuchen essen!"

Der Kunstbetrieb kommt nie ohne Selbstbetrug aus. Er besteht aus vielen engagierten Menschen, die Kunst schaffen und verbreiten und alles für sie geben – und ist gleichzeitig Teil eines globalen Marktes, auf dem zunehmend die Superreichen den Ton angeben. Der Kunstbetrieb ist ein Ort der Kritik, des Widerstands und voller großartiger Ideen, Werke und Visionen. Auch die Forderungen und Nöte der Protestierenden in Paris, die Ausgrenzung von Migranten und die Gewalt und Kriminalität auf den Straßen finden Resonanz in der Kunst, können reflektiert und bearbeitet werden. Doch gleichzeitig ist die Kunst eine Spielwiese für Menschen, die Nutznießer eines Systems sind, das nicht aufhört, Geld von unten nach oben umzuverteilen.

Es ist extrem schade, dass die Art Basel Paris nun zwei Tage früher schließen muss – und auch, dass ausgerechnet zwei von drei Publikumstagen wegfallen. Viele Künstlerinnen und Künstler sowie Galeristinnen und Galeristen haben hart an ihren Präsentationen gearbeitet, die nun von weniger Menschen gesehen werden können. Andererseits: Es würde sich schrecklich anfühlen, eine Ausstellung zu veranstalten oder zu besuchen, die mit Polizeigewalt geschützt werden muss.

Die Soziologie weiß, dass in ungleichen Gesellschaften nicht nur die Armen unglücklich sind, sondern auch die Reichen. Das Leben in gated communities macht keinen Spaß. Und wenn draußen Demonstrierende die Bezahlbarkeit von Wohnen, Essen und Bildung einfordern, fühlt man sich in der Luxuswelt der Kunst manchmal wie Marie Antoinette: "Sie haben kein Brot? Sollen sie doch Kuchen essen!" Wie das für sie ausging, wissen wir.

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“看到自己当年那个菜鸟导演的样子真的挺让人脚趾抠地的，因为那是20年以前，当时我在展现自信和强势方面还没那么熟练，”科波拉说道。“我爸爸总是说：‘你得把“开拍”两个字喊得更大声点，’他担心大家不会认真对待我。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我发现了一个装满差评的盒子，里面全是一个接一个可怕的评论，它们的标题非常搞笑，比如《一场皇室混乱》，而且全都是由男性撰写的，”科波拉说道。“这就好比因为[这部电影]满是花边和女性化元素，所以就被认为只能是轻浮的东西而遭到贬低，我认为这恰恰体现了当时[电影界]对待女性视角的一种不同态度。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管恶评如潮，但科波拉坚称关于《绝代艳后》在戛纳电影节首映时遭到嘘声的报道被严重夸大了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“戛纳的事被夸大了；根本没那么戏剧化，”科波拉说道。“当时有一小撮英国记者开始发出嘘声，然后在记者会上，他们说：‘你们被嘘了。’于是这件事就传了出去，到处都是诸如‘在戛纳遭嘘’之类的头条新闻。而我们当时还觉得我们的放映反响极好呢。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在播客中，科波拉谈到《绝代艳后》如何成为她迄今为止拍摄最艰难的一部电影；该片繁杂的后勤压力——在凡尔赛历史博物馆拍摄并伴随着大量的服装更换——几乎让她崩溃，她承认自己曾一度坚信自己再也不想当电影人了。科波拉很喜欢《黑暗之心》——她经常引用父亲在制作《现代启示录》期间情绪崩溃时说的那句“我要拿个‘F’ ”——她也深知埃莉诺能够进入丈夫和女儿的片场，这是绝大多数纪录片导演永远无法企及的特权。", "text": "“我绝对不会向任何人敞开心扉，也绝不会如此坦诚、毫无防备地吐露心声，除了我妈妈，”科波拉谈到埃莉诺带着摄像机走进导演休息车、记录下她制作《绝代艳后》最低谷时期的情景如是说。“展示这一切让我觉得很尴尬，但我希望它展现了电影创作的真实一面、你当时真实的感受以及那种自我怀疑。所以我希望年轻的电影人看到这些能有所收获，知道每个人都要经历这一切。”", "translated": "links": [{"text": "Sofia Coppola", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/sofia-coppola/"}, {"text": "Toolkit Podcast", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/p/toolkit-hub/"}, {"text": "Making Marie Antoinette", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/making-marie-antoinette-documentary-movie-review-1235214956/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "According to Sofia, Eleanor was frustrated that the material had only appeared in some promotional marketing materials without being utilized to its full potential. Toward the end of her mother’s life (Eleanor died in 2024 at age 87), she made it known that she wanted her memoir to be published as a book, and for “ Making Marie Antoinette ” to be finished — a process that started during lockdown. Sofia said she “never thought to make” the documentary, but wanted to carry out her mother’s wishes and pay tribute to her with the film , which ended up opening her own eyes in a number of different ways.", "links": [{"text": "Making Marie Antoinette", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/making-marie-antoinette/"}, {"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It’s really cringey to see myself as a baby director because it was 20 years ago and I’m not as confident about being assertive,” said Coppola. “My dad would always say, ‘You have to yell ‘action’ louder,’ he was worried that people wouldn’t take me seriously.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sofia, contrasting herself to her father, Francis, acknowledged she has a very low-key demeanor, something that hasn’t changed over the years, but in rewatching the footage she gained perspective of how much, in just 20 years, people’s attitude around her changed. In a moment from “Making Marie Antoinette,” Sofia is seen having to push back against the need for a scene to be covered from the perspective of Jamie Dornan’s character, as if solely shooting it from the female characters’ perspectives was somehow incomplete."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I think you see me really trying to fight for a female point of view that was unusual at the time,” said Coppola. “Where now it’s like everyone gets it, but you can see me struggling to try to make that clear.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MA_Eleanor-2_3000dpi_Credit_Sofia-Coppola.jpeg?w=650", "alt": "", "caption": "Eleanor Coppola shooting ‘Making Marie Antoinette’", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In retrospect, Coppola also believes the same applied to male critics, having recently revisited the scathing critical response her film initially received."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I found a box a pile of bad reviews, and they’re just like one terrible review after the other, and they had really funny headlines like, ‘A Royal Mess,’ and they were all written by men,” said Coppola. “And it was [as if] because [the film] was frilly and feminine, then it had to be fluff and dismissed, and I think that just was sort [of the] attitude — [it] was different then about a woman’s point of view [in movies].”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Despite the bad reviews, Coppola insists the reports of the “Marie Antoinette” getting booed at its Cannes Film Festival premiere were completely overblown."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The thing at Cannes got exaggerated; it wasn’t that dramatic,” said Coppola. “There was a little group of English journalists that started booing, and then they, at the press conference, said, ‘You got booed.’ So then it came out, all these headlines, ‘Booed in Cannes,’ or whatever. We thought we had a great screening.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Back in 2006, Coppola had anticipated receiving some pushback at Cannes — a young American director taking French history, “and turning it on its head, and doing it from the point of view of this villain, and making her human” was something she expected would rub some the wrong way. She took some glee in the film being rebellious, imbued with punk spirit. But she was caught off guard by the response to her anachronistic use of a 1980s post-punk, new wave soundtrack, which included songs from Siouxsie & the Banshees, Bow Wow Wow, The Strokes, New Order, and Aphex Twin."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MA_800dpi_18_Credit_Sofia-Coppola.jpg?w=650", "alt": "'Making Marie Antoinette'", "caption": "‘Making Marie Antoinette’ Sofia Coppola", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I’d rather do stuff that people hate and love than just [get] a mediocre response; it would be boring to do safe, but I was surprised that the contemporary music — that hadn’t been done a lot before. It just seems weird that that was shocking at the time, or offensive. Now, it’s like you don’t even think twice [about using a non-period-accurate needle drop],” said Coppola, who, along with her composer (and husband) Thomas Mars (frontman for the band Phoenix) and longtime music supervisor Randall Poster, was praised for use of anachronistic music in Coppola’s 2023 film “Priscilla.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While on the podcast, Coppola talked about how “Marie Antoinette” was, by far, her most difficult shoot; The stress of the film’s logistics — shooting at the Versailles historical museum with extensive costume changes — nearly broke her, admitting there were times she was convinced she no longer wanted to be a filmmaker. Coppola, who loves “Hearts of Darkness” — and often quotes her father’s “I’m gonna get an ‘F’” meltdown in the middle of making “Apocalypse Now” — also understands the value of Eleanor gaining access that most documentarians never could to both her husband’s and daughter’s sets.", "links": [{"text": "“I’m gonna get an ‘F’” meltdown in the middle of making “Apocalypse Now”", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=psmvOa8F9hY"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I would never open up and I would never talk so honestly, and be vulnerable like that except for my mom,” said Coppola about Eleanor coming into the director’s trailer with her camera at her lowest points while making “Marie Antoinette.” “It’s embarrassing for me to show that, but I hope it shows a real aspect of filmmaking and what you’re really feeling at the time and the self-doubt. So I hope to younger filmmakers it’s helpful to see that everybody goes through that.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet the most personal revelation from working on “Making Marie Antoinette” for Sofia was understanding what it was like for her proud mother to watch her then-34-year-old daughter orchestrate this massive production. After Eleanor passed away, editor Aaron Matthews found the parts in her journal that corresponded to being on the “Marie Antoinette” set — those entries would later become the documentary’s voice-over (read by Eleanor’s close friend, actress Diane Lane). In her journal, Eleanor reflected that when she was Sofia’s age, she already had three kids and felt like she had to sacrifice her own creative career for her family."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“She always felt like she wasn’t able to do her full creative work because of being a mother and wife. article_text:
While director Sofia Coppola was laboring on “ Marie Antoinette, ” documentarian Eleanor Coppola , the director’s mother, shot 80 hours of behind-the-scenes footage. Eleanor had done this before, most notably for her groundbreaking 1991 documentary “Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse,” which served as an all-access pass to her husband, Francis Ford Coppola , laying it all on the line to produce “Apocalypse Now.” But unlike that project, Eleanor’s “ Marie Antoinette ” footage has gone untouched.

That is until 2020, when Sofia and her family moved back to Francis and Eleanor’s Northern California Vineyard Estate during the COVID-19 lockdown.

“We were all at home in Napa, and my mom said, ‘Let’s get the footage out and look at it,’” said Sofia Coppola , while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast to discuss both the 20th anniversary re-release of “Marie Antoinette” and Eleanor’s documentary “ Making Marie Antoinette .” “It was the first time I had ever seen it, and I didn’t realize how much footage she had.”

According to Sofia, Eleanor was frustrated that the material had only appeared in some promotional marketing materials without being utilized to its full potential. Toward the end of her mother’s life (Eleanor died in 2024 at age 87), she made it known that she wanted her memoir to be published as a book, and for “ Making Marie Antoinette ” to be finished — a process that started during lockdown. Sofia said she “never thought to make” the documentary, but wanted to carry out her mother’s wishes and pay tribute to her with the film , which ended up opening her own eyes in a number of different ways.

“It’s really cringey to see myself as a baby director because it was 20 years ago and I’m not as confident about being assertive,” said Coppola. “My dad would always say, ‘You have to yell ‘action’ louder,’ he was worried that people wouldn’t take me seriously.”

Sofia, contrasting herself to her father, Francis, acknowledged she has a very low-key demeanor, something that hasn’t changed over the years, but in rewatching the footage she gained perspective of how much, in just 20 years, people’s attitude around her changed. In a moment from “Making Marie Antoinette,” Sofia is seen having to push back against the need for a scene to be covered from the perspective of Jamie Dornan’s character, as if solely shooting it from the female characters’ perspectives was somehow incomplete.

“I think you see me really trying to fight for a female point of view that was unusual at the time,” said Coppola. “Where now it’s like everyone gets it, but you can see me struggling to try to make that clear.”

In retrospect, Coppola also believes the same applied to male critics, having recently revisited the scathing critical response her film initially received.

“I found a box a pile of bad reviews, and they’re just like one terrible review after the other, and they had really funny headlines like, ‘A Royal Mess,’ and they were all written by men,” said Coppola. “And it was [as if] because [the film] was frilly and feminine, then it had to be fluff and dismissed, and I think that just was sort [of the] attitude — [it] was different then about a woman’s point of view [in movies].”

Despite the bad reviews, Coppola insists the reports of the “Marie Antoinette” getting booed at its Cannes Film Festival premiere were completely overblown.

“The thing at Cannes got exaggerated; it wasn’t that dramatic,” said Coppola. “There was a little group of English journalists that started booing, and then they, at the press conference, said, ‘You got booed.’ So then it came out, all these headlines, ‘Booed in Cannes,’ or whatever. We thought we had a great screening.”

Back in 2006, Coppola had anticipated receiving some pushback at Cannes — a young American director taking French history, “and turning it on its head, and doing it from the point of view of this villain, and making her human” was something she expected would rub some the wrong way. She took some glee in the film being rebellious, imbued with punk spirit. But she was caught off guard by the response to her anachronistic use of a 1980s post-punk, new wave soundtrack, which included songs from Siouxsie & the Banshees, Bow Wow Wow, The Strokes, New Order, and Aphex Twin.

“I’d rather do stuff that people hate and love than just [get] a mediocre response; it would be boring to do safe, but I was surprised that the contemporary music — that hadn’t been done a lot before. It just seems weird that that was shocking at the time, or offensive. Now, it’s like you don’t even think twice [about using a non-period-accurate needle drop],” said Coppola, who, along with her composer (and husband) Thomas Mars (frontman for the band Phoenix) and longtime music supervisor Randall Poster, was praised for use of anachronistic music in Coppola’s 2023 film “Priscilla.”

While on the podcast, Coppola talked about how “Marie Antoinette” was, by far, her most difficult shoot; The stress of the film’s logistics — shooting at the Versailles historical museum with extensive costume changes — nearly broke her, admitting there were times she was convinced she no longer wanted to be a filmmaker. Coppola, who loves “Hearts of Darkness” — and often quotes her father’s “I’m gonna get an ‘F’” meltdown in the middle of making “Apocalypse Now” — also understands the value of Eleanor gaining access that most documentarians never could to both her husband’s and daughter’s sets.

“I would never open up and I would never talk so honestly, and be vulnerable like that except for my mom,” said Coppola about Eleanor coming into the director’s trailer with her camera at her lowest points while making “Marie Antoinette.” “It’s embarrassing for me to show that, but I hope it shows a real aspect of filmmaking and what you’re really feeling at the time and the self-doubt. So I hope to younger filmmakers it’s helpful to see that everybody goes through that.”

Yet the most personal revelation from working on “Making Marie Antoinette” for Sofia was understanding what it was like for her proud mother to watch her then-34-year-old daughter orchestrate this massive production. After Eleanor passed away, editor Aaron Matthews found the parts in her journal that corresponded to being on the “Marie Antoinette” set — those entries would later become the documentary’s voice-over (read by Eleanor’s close friend, actress Diane Lane). In her journal, Eleanor reflected that when she was Sofia’s age, she already had three kids and felt like she had to sacrifice her own creative career for her family.

“She always felt like she wasn’t able to do her full creative work because of being a mother and wife. She just said how different her generation was, and she was really encouraging and happy to see me being able to do both,” said Coppola. “ I didn’t expect that [in Eleanor’s journals], even though I knew that was something that was a big theme for her. And then also seeing myself as a young director through my mom’s eyes, 20 years later, and now I’m a mother to grown daughters, I see it also as a mother’s perspective, so it was really touching for me.”

The postscript to “Making Marie Antoinette” notes that Eleanor would go on to make “Paris Can Wait” (2016) and “Love Is Love Is Love” (2020).

“She made her first narrative feature film at 80, so she’s the oldest person on record to have made their debut film at 80, which is so cool,” said Coppola. “And she says that seeing me do my work was the inspiration.”

MUBI is releasing both “Making Marie Antoinette” and the remastered “Marie Antoinette” in theaters this weekend, timed to the film’s 20th Anniversary. The remastered “Marie Antoinette” will also be released by Criterion in November.

To hear Sofia Coppola’s full interview, subscribe to the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast on Apple , Spotify , or your favorite podcast platform . You can also watch the full interview on YouTube .

article_text:
三菱一号館美術館 で「 フォンタネージ――イタリアの光・心の風景 」が 2027年1月24日まで開催されています。

広い野原にぽつんとたたずむ人物、柔らかな光に包まれた木立、夕暮れの空。アントニオ・フォンタネージ（1818～1882年）の風景画には、自然の美しさとともに、人間の心の動きが静かに描き込まれています。遠いヨーロッパの風景でありながら、どこか懐かしさを覚える作品が少なくありません。

日本では、明治時代に来日し、工部美術学校で浅井忠や小山正太郎らを指導した「お雇い外国人」として知られるフォンタネージ。1977年の「フォンタネージ、ラグーザと明治前期の美術」も日本近代洋画との関わりを中心とした展覧会であり、画家自身の全貌に触れる機会はこれまで限られていました。

それから約半世紀。三菱一号館美術館での「フォンタネージ――イタリアの光・心の風景」は、イタリア近代風景画の巨匠としてのフォンタネージを初めて主役に据えた日本初の大回顧展です。

日本とイタリアの研究者による共同研究をもとに、初期から晩年までの油彩、素描、版画や関連作家の作品など約200点を通して、その豊かな画業を紹介します。

ヨーロッパ各地で培われた風景画

1818年、イタリア北部のレッジョ・エミリアに生まれたフォンタネージは、若い頃にイタリア独立戦争に参加した経歴を持ちます。その後スイスに移り、ジュネーヴを拠点に画家として活動を始めました。

1855年にはパリでコローやバルビゾン派の画家たちの作品に触れ、1858年には南仏で風景画家フランソワ＝オーギュスト・ラヴィエと出会います。ロンドン滞在中にはターナーやコンスタブルの絵画も研究しました。

こうした経験を通して、自然を忠実に描写しながら、そこに自身の感情や詩情を重ねる風景表現を深めていきます。

初期の《ブジェイ高原》や《水車小屋》《静寂》などには、その試みをうかがうことができます。さらに《フィレンツェの旧市場》などの都市風景では、街路や建築、そこに暮らす人々の姿にも目を向けました。

パリのサロンへの出品を通じてミレーやローザ・ボヌールらの作品に触れ、農民や家畜を主題とする絵画にも取り組みます。《労働》などからは、自然と人間の営みを一体としてとらえようとする姿勢が読み取れます。

風景画に描かれた「孤独」

フォンタネージの風景画を語るうえで欠かせないのが「孤独」という主題です。

《十一月》には、晩秋の広大な風景の中に羊飼いの少女がひとり描かれています。周囲には静かな自然が広がり、小さな人物の姿がかえってその広さを感じさせます。

画面から伝わってくるのは、寂しさであると同時に、自然の中に身を置く人間の静かな心情です。フォンタネージはこうした孤独な人物を繰り返し描き、1875年には《孤独》と題した作品も制作しました。

広々とした風景の中に人間を小さく描くことで、自然と人との距離、そして言葉にならない感情を表現する。そこには寂しさを否定するのではなく、静かに受け入れるようなまなざしが感じられます。フォンタネージにとって風景画とは、自分の心を映し出す手段でもあったのでしょう。

光と大気の変化をとらえた《四月》と《雲》

自然の変化を通して感情を表現しようとする姿勢は、光や大気を描いた作品にも表れています。

《四月》は、縦約1.7㍍、横約2.5㍍に及ぶ大作です。雲が太陽を遮った瞬間、平原に虹色の光が差し込む様子が描かれています。フォンタネージは刻々と変化する光や気象に関心を寄せ、それを人間の感情の起伏と結びつけて考えていました。

晩年の代表作《雲》は、さらに大きな縦2㍍、横約3㍍の作品です。帰国後のトリノで制作され、同年の全国美術展に出品されましたが、当時は賛否両論を呼びました。

晩年のフォンタネージはパレットナイフを大胆に用い、作品の修正を繰り返しながら、画家自身が考える「真実」の風景を追い求めました。《雲》はその探求を知るうえで重要な作品です。

本展の特別章では、《四月》と《雲》を手がかりに、フォンタネージの風景表現と日本近代洋画との関係も紹介されています。

「天然を師として」日本に残した教え

1876年、58歳で来日したフォンタネージは、明治政府が設立した工部美術学校の画学教師に就任しました。

滞在期間は約2年。体調の悪化や政府の財政難、学校運営をめぐる問題などから1878年に帰国しましたが、教え子たちに大きな影響を与えました。

離日に際して弟子たちに贈ったとされる言葉があります。

「今後は一途に天然を師として勉強せよ」

自然を注意深く観察し、そこから学ぶことを何よりも大切にした画家らしい言葉です。浅井忠《徳川家の霊廟Ⅰ（寺の入り口Ⅰ）》や小山正太郎《秋景図》などからは、その教えが日本の若い画家たちにどのように受け継がれたのかをたどることができます。

さらにフォンタネージの芸術は、ジョヴァンニ・セガンティーニやジュゼッペ・ペリッツァ・ダ・ヴォルペード、カルロ・カッラら後世のイタリア人画家たちにも影響を及ぼしました。

絵画と建築、二人の「お雇い外国人」

本展会場・三菱一号館美術館にも、フォンタネージと共通する歴史があります。旧三菱一号館を設計した英国人建築家ジョサイア・コンドル（Josiah Conder、1852～1920）も、明治政府に招かれた「お雇い外国人」のひとりでした。

コンドルが来日したのは1877年。フォンタネージの来日からわずか1年後のことです。工部大学校で辰野金吾らを育てたコンドルと、工部美術学校で浅井忠らを指導したフォンタネージ。絵画と建築という異なる分野で、日本の近代化に貢献した二人が、ほぼ同じ時期に日本で教育に携わっていたことも興味深い事実です。

日本人の感性に響く、心の風景

フォンタネージの作品を実際に観ていると、異国の風景でありながら、どこか懐かしさを覚えます。柔らかな光、季節の移ろい、自然の中に感じる静けさ。《十一月》に描かれた孤独さえも、決して冷たいものではなく、見る人の心に穏やかに寄り添ってくるようです。

こうした自然へのまなざしや、風景に自身の感情を重ねる表現は、四季の変化を愛で、もの寂しさの中にも美しさを見いだしてきた日本人の感性とも通じるものがあるのでしょう。

フォンタネージの絵画には、人の目を驚かせるような劇的な場面よりも、日常の何気ない風景を大切にする姿勢が感じられます。壮大な光景を描いた大作にも、静かな農村風景にも、自然と人間を見つめる温かなまなざしが通っています。

ひとつひとつの作品をゆっくりと眺めていると、風景の中を流れる時間まで感じられるようです。孤独や寂しさも含めて、自然とともにある人間の姿を優しく受け止めてくれる。そんなフォンタネージの風景画に包まれ、心が落ち着いていくような心地よさを味わえる展覧会でした。

三菱一号館美術館・主任学芸員の杉山菜穂子氏から美術展ナビの読者にメッセージが届いています。 「本展は教育者として知られるフォンタネージの画業の全貌をご覧いただける貴重な展覧会です。当館では、建物の制約から一階の展示室にフォンタネージの大作《四月》と《雲》を展示しております。傑作2点を一緒に鑑賞できるまたとない機会となりますので、迫力ある展示をお楽しみ頂ければと思います」 （ライター・中村剛士＝青い日記帳）

article_text:
The American Film Market set an inaugural New Global Screen Economy Summit on opening day that will examine a proposed federal production tax incentive, and unveiled an expanded lineup of speakers across 45+ sessions.

AFM runs Nov. 10–15 at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles..

The new summit will also delve into the creator economy, new IP sources and the evolving studio system.

Panelists over the five days are from UTA, CAA, the MPA, Artists Equity, Alamo Drafthouse, Trafalgar Releasing, Ashland Hill, Cineverse, Crunchroll, Gersh, Lionsgate, Range Select, Rentrak, Spooky Pictures, Project X, Wrapbook and more. Speakers include AGC’s Stuart Ford, Evan Shapiro, Amy Baer, Wesley Wang, and Tyler Chou.

Related Stories

Brittany O'Grady To Star In Thriller 'State Of Emergency' For 'House Of The Dragon' Director Greg Yaitanes & FilmNation -- AFM

Holt McCallany Serial Killer Thriller 'Paradise Disturbed' Heads To AFM With Stoic; See The First-Look Image

AFM’s 47th edition spans the Fairmont Century Plaza, AMC Century City 15 and The Pavilion.

Watch on Deadline

“Our industry is undergoing a fundamental transformation, and while the pace of change can feel overwhelming, the opportunities are incredibly exciting,” said Jackie Brenneman, president and CEO of the Independent Film & Television Alliance, which produces AFM.

“From how stories are discovered and what gets made to how content reaches audiences and the renewed excitement around the theatrical experience, nearly every part of our business is being reimagined. We’re expanding AFM to bring new voices and perspectives into the conversation alongside the industry leaders and innovators driving this change. This complements the tremendous business and dealmaking activity at the heart of the Market while creating more opportunities to connect, exchange ideas and discover new opportunities together.”

The kickoff session Nov. 10 is called The New Federal Production Incentive : A Turning Point for U.S. Production with Steven Paul, chairman-CEO of SP Media Group; SP Media Group president Scott Karol; and Josh Rogin, SVP of Federal Affairs for the MPA.

Another new addition this year is AFM House, which will feature four days of conversations, presentations and live demos of emerging technologies. Home to the expanded AFM Innovation Hub, presented in partnership with Marché du Film’s Cannes Next, AFM House will host the North American debut of the Cinemas Club, bringing together industry leaders to explore the future of theatrical exhibition and moviegoing.

article_text:
How do you manage not to act starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Harrison Ford? TopTramp That’s where my acting comes in – I pretend that I don’t know how famous they are. Every actor really wants a leader. They want someone who knows the script really well, has a plan for how the scene is going to be executed, and – in the case of comedy – knows how to make it funny. The last thing any of those guys wants is someone coming in starstruck and wide-eyed. So I use my acting skills to pretend I’m not starstruck and treat them like normal people.

Your Fake Doctors, Real Friends podcast was a real help through lockdown. You were very emotionally open and personal; it was like catching up with friends. I still think about your line that making it in acting, even if you’re talented and good-looking, is like winning the lottery. Do you think that early 00s Zach Braff would make it in the present day the way you did? KamesJ Back then, the broadcast networks were making so many pilots, at least it was work for people. Now, I think it’s a much harder landscape to break through. I firmly believe that you can be talented and good-looking, but success is still like winning the lottery. I know plenty of brilliant actors whose lottery ticket hasn’t come up yet. I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years, so I’ve always felt very lucky.

And as far as the podcast, that’s so great to hear. We didn’t plan to start it during Covid, but it became a nice sort of warm hug for people who wanted a little bit of nostalgia. Donald [Faison, who plays Dr Turk] and I loved getting together, making each other laugh and reminiscing. So much so that we’re actually bringing it back.

Have you thought about Garden State 2? Haggisneepsnfatties We did an anniversary concert for the soundtrack last year – we got most of the bands together and did a charity show for the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles – and that was really cool. Natalie Portman was there. I had told her that people have come to me about doing a musical of the movie. I love musicals, but I’ve always thought: “I don’t know if that I want to do that.” Then she said: “Why don’t you do it with the songs from the soundtrack?” It’s funny, because I never thought of that. I haven’t taken any steps to make it a reality, but I do daydream of somehow using the music that people love so much from the soundtrack to make it into a musical.

When you agreed to join the cast of BoJack Horseman , how did you feel about your character having such a grisly end? topfoot I love the show, so it was so fun to play a cartoonish version of myself, and I just did whatever they said. I never said: “Don’t kill me that way. Don’t have Jessica Biel feast on my carcass,” or whatever the hell it was.

How much fun was it playing a small role in Arrested Development – to my mind the funniest, cleverest and silliest of all the US sitcoms? Manofthesouth It was amazing, especially because I didn’t know I was going to be a never-nude until I got the script. In the world of Arrested Development, a never-nude is someone – mainly Tobias – who can never be fully naked, even in the shower, so he wears denim short-shorts.

Scrubs and Arrested Development were both doing really well. Jason Bateman and I were at some big event with the heads of both networks – we were NBC, they were Fox. We were laughing, saying: “It’d be fun if we each guested on each other’s show, but the networks would never let us do that.” Then we realised: “They’re all here. Let’s just go ask them.” They said “Sure,” so I guested on Arrested and Jason did an episode of Scrubs as an ostrich farmer.

Who would you most like to cast in Dr Acula : The Movie – JD’s vampire-doctor screenplay in Scrubs? PickleMan Michael B Jordan and Leonardo DiCaprio, if we’re in the fantasy where we’re going to make an amazing, huge-budget version. Remember at the end of Pee-wee’s Big Adventure when they make the movie of his life and cast beautiful movie stars, and Pee-wee ends up as a bellhop? That’s the version of Dr Acula I want: megastars, while Donald and I are just in the background.

You’ve had huge success whether you’re acting, writing or directing. If you were to pick one standout pinch-me moment, what would it be? Turnipsnitzel Morgan Freeman saying yes to my film was one of those great moments. So was standing in the back of the Eccles theatre in Park City when Garden State premiered, thinking: “Holy shit, how did this happen?”

When I got Scrubs, I was waiting tables. I put my Motorola StarTAC phone on the passenger seat as I was driving home from the final callback, and was just eyeing it to see if it was going to ring. Then it rang, I pulled over, called my parents, then I called the manager of the restaurant. She said: “I’m so happy for you, babe, but you got to work tonight still.” I said: “Oh, don’t worry, I’m coming in.” So I worked the whole shift knowing I probably wouldn’t be waiting tables for a couple of years.

If you were on a plane and there was an announcement asking if there’s a doctor on board, would you put your hand up? MrSOBaldrick Absolutely not. I don’t know anything. I really don’t. We have the most amazing consultants on set, including this wonderful nurse who’s just a badass. She shows us what to do and tells us what the hell we’re saying. Anyone who thinks we know anything for real is crazy.

Scrubs taught me a lot about illness, life and death. Did it do the same for you? waydgroods I was so young when we did the original series that I don’t think I had any experience with loss and being in hospitals and grief. In the years since, I’ve lost so many people. I’ve sat in hospital and ICU waiting rooms, waiting with bated breath for the doctor to come in with good or bad news. I’ve seen how the nurses run the whole hospital. I’ve witnessed it first-hand in a way I hadn’t as a young man. So I think now I have even more respect. I feel more like I’m playing a superhero as the guy who’s the chief of medicine at an underfunded hospital who’s meant to be a particularly badass doctor.

Does your hair have its own agent? Dr_J_A_Zoidberg My hair’s agent is that I take a shower at night and then I go to sleep on it and you get magical bedhead.

article_text:
Editor’s note: T his story contains details of alleged sexual offenses that readers may find distressing

Russell Brand told one of his fans to “clean up the mess” after allegedly anally raping her at his home in north London, a court has been told.

On a busy day at London’s Southwark Crown Court, the jury heard from three of Brand’s six accusers. The court was played a 2024 video recording of a police interview with one woman, whom we are calling Complainant 5 (C5) as she has a lifelong right to anonymity . During the two-hour-long interview, C5 was frequently in tears and distressed as she relived her alleged encounter with Brand.

Related Stories

Russell Brand Accuser Says She Reported Comedian To Channel 4 In 2009 After He Allegedly Lay His Head On Her Lap & Demanded Massage

Russell Brand Accuser Alleges Witnesses Were Present When He "Grabbed My Face" & "Pushed His Body Against Mine" At Radio Station

The Despicable Me star faces three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of indecent assault based on allegations made by six women . He will set out his defense later in the trial, denies all charges, and has pleaded not guilty.

Watch on Deadline

C5, who thought Brand was “interesting, articulate and intelligent about things that others would shy away from,” said she met Brand at one of his comedy gigs in 2009 at the Hammersmith Apollo. She was “invited upstairs for drinks,” after which she consensually performed oral sex on him but told him she didn’t want to have penetrative sex.

She said he took her number, “thought I’d never hear from him again,” but Brand kept messaging her and soon after she agreed to go to his house in Hampstead, north London.

She was driven to his home by a driver, let in by an associate of Brand’s and was told, “Russell’s on the phone to America.” Brand then came downstairs and told her, “This is the best decision you’ve ever made,” she said during the police interview, which was played to the jury to avoid C5 having to retell her story in the courtroom. Deadline has been following the trial live via a closed video stream from the courtroom.

C5 alleged that Brand’s demeanor changed when they were kissing on his bed and he suddenly said, “You need to have a shower because your hair smells funny,” which “didn’t sound kind” but made her “feel like I was dirty.”

At first, C5 alleged she and Brand had consensual penetrative sex and Brand was using a condom. “I didn’t enjoy the experience because I felt like somebody was just f**king a hole,” she added. “I could have been anyone. It didn’t matter who I was.”

After having consensual sex for some time, C5 alleged Brand “turned me onto my front,” and she assumed he wanted to continue vaginal sex. Instead, she said he inserted his fingers into her anus before anally raping her, which she said was extremely painful.

C5 alleged Brand said to her, “I want you to feel my cum,” at which point he ejaculated inside her anus and she realized he had removed his condom.

After he was finished, she alleged Brand “looked absolutely horrified” and told her, “You need to clean up the mess that you’ve made.” He then left the room and his associate told her that Brand was performing another gig shortly and “whenever you are ready you can leave.”

C5 was in tears during the police interview when she said: “I went there knowing I would have sex with him and what I mean is vaginal penetrative sex. I went knowing that would happen. I want to make that clear because I’ve struggled to accept what happened to me because I went there knowingly and willingly.”

“He did not act like he’d done anything wrong”

That evening, she said she told her flatmate what had happened and was in so much pain she had to “sit on an ice cube tray.”

She was later told she had an anal tear and became convinced she had contracted HIV, for which she tested negative. “I wanted to just leave it all behind,” she told police. “I thought maybe he does that all the time. He did not act like he’d done anything wrong.”

Since the incident, C5 said she has struggled with alcohol addiction and went to rehab in 2023, during which time she opened up about the incident. Around that time, Channel 4 aired its Russell Brand: In Plain Sight documentary, which was a catalyst for her going to police.

“I’ve tried not thinking about it and it hasn’t worked, so whatever happens after this [police interview], I know I’ve sat in a room and said what happened to me,” she explained. “I just don’t want to die knowing that what he did to me I have not said to the right people.”

“I carried the feeling of guilt and shame”

C5 is the final Brand accuser to give evidence and took to the stand for questioning on Wednesday. All of the accusers came forward after watching the Channel 4 documentary, but none of them know each other, the prosecution has said.

Under questioning from Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter, C5, who gave evidence to the court from behind a screen, said she had “carried the burden” and “carried the feeling of guilt and shame” for years after the alleged attack.

She was repeatedly pressed by Winter on whether she had in fact consented to anal sex as well as vaginal sex with Brand, but continued to deny that this was the case.

“Just because you go somewhere willingly, that does not mean the outcome at the end is [necessarily] consensual,” she said. “I did not make the decision to have anal sex with Mr. Brand. I did not make that decision. We never had a conversation about anal sex.”

The summer after the alleged rape took place, the court heard that C5 saw Brand from a distance at an event she was working at during the Edinburgh Festival. She said he texted her and she replied asking why he was messaging her, and Brand responded, “Because you’re dirty and I wanna push you further.” C5 said she then responded by saying, “I think you pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal,” to which Brand then quickly apologized and the text conversation ended.

Pushed by Winter on why she didn’t tell Brand he had raped her, C5 said: “To give you that answer is really difficult.”

She was also pressed by Winter on how much she “adored” Brand, with Winter putting forward the idea several times that she was “obsessed” with Brand before she first met him at the Hammersmith Apollo.

“You knew he was extremely sexually active with multiple women?,” asked Winter, to which C5 replied: “Correct.”

“You knew he had won The Sun newspaper’s ‘Shagger of the Year’ award three years running,” Winter then asked.

“I don’t think I was aware of that,” replied C5.

The evidence from Brand’s accusers is now over and the court will return tomorrow with witnesses. The court has been told repeatedly that Brand declined to answer questions when interviewed by police. He instead relied on a prepared statement, in which he claimed that he did not recall meeting the women and did not remember their names. He said any sexual contact was consensual.

The trial continues.

article_text:
Wicker stars Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, and Elizabeth Debicki attended the Los Angeles premiere of their film at the DGA Theater.

The cast and producers at the event also included Tim Headington, Justin Lothrop, Eleanor Wilson, Alex Huston Fischer, and Brad Zimmerman.

Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson wrote and directed Wicker, based on the short story “The Wicker Husband” by Ursula Wills. The film premieres in U.S. theaters on October 23.

RELATED: ‘Nocturne’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Liev Schreiber, Zazie Beetz, Chrissy Metz & More

Wicker is an audacious comedic fable about sex, marriage, and the absurdities of social convention. The film tells the love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband to be made by the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage).

When her wicker husband (Alexander Skarsgård) proves more spectacular than she ever imagined, his soulful spirit and unique prowess awaken something inside her, setting off a wave of jealousy, fascination, and upheaval that threatens the very fabric of village life.

RELATED: ‘Klara And The Sun’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams, Florence Pugh, Aran Murphy & More

Wicker was brought to life through craftsmanship, including cinematography by Lol Crawley ( The Brutalist ), production design by Renátó Cseh ( Poor Things ), costumes by Tóth András Dániel and Attila Godena-Juhász, and a score by Anna Meredith ( Eight Grade ).

Skarsgård’s title character was realized through a fully practical suit, created by Joe Dunckley and Wētā Workshop ( Avatar , The Lord of the Rings ).

Wicker producers include Ed Sinclair, Tom Carver, Olivia Colman, Justin Lothrop, Brent Stiefel, Brad Zimmerman, David Michod, Andrea Cornwell, Oliver Kassman, Tim Headington, Lia Buman, Ryan Heller, Michael Bloom

RELATED: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Character Posters: Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke, Glenn Close & More

title_original: Women Artists Are Having a Moment in Prints. What Does Market Data Reveal?
editorial_title_zh: 女性艺术家正在版画领域迎来高光时刻。市场数据揭示了什么？
editorial_excerpt_zh: 最近的销售表明，市场差距并不像看上去那样具有可预测性。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在过去的几年里，各大博物馆越来越关注那些创作延伸至版画领域的女性艺术家。费城艺术博物馆在2025年推出了“朱莉·麦赫雷图：聚焦”（Julie Mehretu : In Focus），此前该馆收藏了这位艺术家的两套不朽版画系列。艺术博览会上也同样能看到对女性版画家的关注。2025年IFPDA版画艺博会委托米卡莱娜·托马斯（Mickalene Thomas）在纽约公园大道军械库创作了一件特定场域装置，探索版画创作的可能性，而劳拉·欧文斯（Laura Owens）、琼·霍尔（Joan Hall）和露易丝·布尔乔亚（Louise Bourgeois）等艺术家今年则成为了该艺博会各个展位上的焦点。", "links": [{"text": "took center stage across the fair’s booths this year", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/art-world/the-women-defining-printmaking-at-the-2026-ifpda-print-fair-2763982"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Thomas-framed-856x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "米卡莱娜·托马斯（Mickalene Thomas），《内部：带黑鸟的壁炉》（Interior: Fireplace with Blackbird），2016年。桑德斯·沃特福德纸本综合媒介拼贴，含丝网印刷、木刻、数码版画、蚀刻、金箔、木饰面和植绒。图片来源：Artnet拍卖行。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但是，女性版画家的市场是否跟上了这种机构层面的关注？为了弄清这一点，我们查阅了Artnet价格数据库的拍卖结果，而得出的发现比单纯的价格对比所显示的要更为复杂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在2022年至2026年间总计21.8亿美元的版画及多版原作（editions）销售额中，女性艺术家的作品仅占7%，但这一差距是由数量而非价值驱动的。在此期间，男性艺术家的多版原作上拍量达到了286,970件，而女性艺术家则为24,144件。仅就价格而言，女性版画的平均售价仅略低于男性，其成交率更高，且高于最高估价的成交结果也更为频繁。对于成功登上拍卖场的女性艺术家而言，市场显然是存在的；代表权和可获得性才是真正的障碍。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/helen-frankenthaler-contentment-island-prints-and-multiples-zoom_398_500.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "海伦·弗兰肯塔勒（Helen Frankenthaler），《甘美岛》（Contentment Island），2004年。Rives BFK纸本彩色丝网印刷。图片来源：Artnet拍卖行", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关于性别差距更复杂的全貌", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "已发表的研究记录了更广泛的艺术品拍卖市场中显著的性别价格差距。蕾妮·亚当斯（Renée Adams）、罗曼·克劳斯尔（Roman Kräussl）、马可·纳沃内（Marco Navone）和帕特里克·韦尔维梅伦（Patrick Verwijmeren）在2021年进行的一项研究依据了49个国家的190万笔拍卖交易，发现女性艺术家的绘画作品平均比男性艺术家的绘画作品售价低42.1%。但这种差距同样适用于版画和多版原作吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "涵盖2022至2026年的Artnet价格数据库数据表明，答案并非那么简单。在此期间，女性艺术家版画及多版原作的拍卖中位价约为2,016美元（含买方佣金），略高于男性版画及多版原作1,937美元的中位价。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "女性版画在其他衡量标准上的表现也略胜一筹。在同一时期，女性艺术家拍品的成交率为78.8%，而男性艺术家的成交率为75.2%。此外，有43.1%的女性拍品成交价高于其最高估价，相比之下男性拍品这一比例为41.1%。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Women-Artists-Prints-Lead-at-Auction-1024x683.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些数据让那种认为女性版画在二级市场上持续落后于男性的假设变得复杂。它们表明，尽管平均价格和总体销售额存在差异，但女性作品在多项衡量标准上都表现出了竞争力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "谁在引领女性版画市场？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "更仔细地审视哪些女性艺术家在推动版画市场，会揭示故事的另一层含义。从2022年到2026年，草间弥生（Yayoi Kusama）在拍卖总销售额方面依然稳居领先地位，这既突显出市场对她作品的强劲需求，也彰显了她版画创作惊人的多产性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但总销售额同时也是衡量市场体量的指标：那些拥有大量版画和多版原作、且频繁出现在拍卖场上的艺术家，比那些多版原作产量较少或交易不那么频繁的艺术家拥有更多积累销售额的机会。因此，这些排名呈现的是艺术家市场的规模与活跃度，而不是对个别作品价值的直接对比。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/julie-mehretu-unclosed-prints-and-multiples.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "朱莉·麦赫雷图（Julie Mehretu），《未闭合》（Unclosed），2007年。萨默塞特纸本彩色蚀刻、凹版和干刻。图片来源：Artnet拍卖行", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了草间弥生，最近的数据显示，老牌版画家与吸引了大量关注的当代艺术家形成了一种交融。海伦·弗兰肯塔勒、凯特·科勒维茨（Käthe article_text:
Over the past few years, museums have increasingly spotlighted women artists whose practices extend into printmaking. The Philadelphia Museum of Art presented “ Julie Mehretu : In Focus” in 2025, following its acquisition of two monumental print series by the artist. The attention on women printmakers has also been seen at art fairs. The 2025 IFPDA Print Fair commissioned Mickalene Thomas to create a site-specific installation exploring the possibilities of printmaking at the Park Avenue Armory in New York, and artists like Laura Owens , Joan Hall , and Louise Bourgeois took center stage across the fair’s booths this year .

Mickalene Thomas, Interior: Fireplace with Blackbird , 2016. Mixed media collage with screenprint, woodcut, digital print, etching, gold leaf, wood veneer, and flocking on Saunders Waterford paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions.

But is the market for women printmakers keeping pace with this institutional attention? To find out, we examined auction results from the Artnet Price Database , and the findings are more complicated than a simple price comparison suggests.

Prints and multiples by women artists account for just 7 percent of the $2.18 billion in combined editions sales between 2022 and 2026, but that gap is driven by volume, not value. In that period, 286,970 editioned works by male artists came to auction, compared with 24,144 by women. On price alone, women’s prints sell for only slightly less on average than men’s, with a higher sell-through rate and more frequent results above high estimate. The market is clearly there for women artists who make it to auction; representation and availability remain the real obstacles.

Helen Frankenthaler, Contentment Island , 2004. Screenprint in colors on Rives BFK paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions

A more complicated picture of the gender gap

Published research has documented a significant gender price gap in the broader art auction market. A 2021 study by Renée Adams , Roman Kräussl , Marco Navone , and Patrick Verwijmeren , based on 1.9 million auction transactions across 49 countries, found that paintings by female artists sold for 42.1 percent less, on average, than paintings by male artists. But does the same disparity hold for prints and editions?

Artnet Price Database data covering 2022–2026 suggests that the answer is not that straightforward. Over this period, the median auction price for prints and multiples by women artists was approximately $2,016, including buyer’s premium, just above the $1,937 median for prints and multiples by men.

Women’s prints also performed slightly better on other measures. Over the same period, 78.8 percent of lots by women artists sold, compared with 75.2 percent of those by men. And 43.1 percent of women’s lots sold above their high estimates, versus 41.1 percent of men’s.

These figures complicate the assumption that women’s prints consistently lag men’s in the secondary market. They suggest that women’s works are performing competitively on several measures, even as differences in average prices and overall sales volume persist.

Who is leading the women’s prints market?

Looking more closely at which women artists are driving the prints market reveals another layer to the story. From 2022 through 2026, Yayoi Kusama remained the clear leader by total auction sales value, underscoring both the strength of demand for her work and the extraordinary prolificacy of her printmaking practice.

But total sales value is also a measure of market volume: Artists with large bodies of prints and multiples appearing regularly at auction have more opportunities to accumulate sales than those whose editions are produced or traded less frequently. For that reason, the rankings offer a picture of the size and activity of an artist’s market rather than a direct comparison of the value of individual works.

Julie Mehretu, Unclosed , 2007. Etching with aquatint and drypoint in colors on Somerset paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions

Beyond Kusama, the recent data shows a mix of established printmakers and contemporary artists attracting significant activity. Helen Frankenthaler , Käthe Kollwitz , Bridget Riley , Vija Celmins , and Barbara Kruger remain among the market’s established names, while Julie Mehretu , Kara Walker , and Tracey Emin have emerged as particularly notable presences in recent years. Between them, they generated approximately $6.7 million in prints and multiples sales between 2022 and 2026, placing them among the leading contemporary women artists in recent years.

The data also points to a deeper historical imbalance. Of the 15 top-performing women printmakers by auction value, only three were born before 1900, and none before 1867. This isn’t necessarily evidence that women weren’t making prints earlier; rather, it reflects how much work may still be needed to bring this material to the market. Over half of these top-performing printmakers are also American, pointing to the democratization efforts of printmaking studios during the Postwar Print Renaissance in the U.S., especially after Tatyana Grosman founded Universal Limited Art Editions in 1957, setting the standard for printmaking in the country.

Taken together, the rankings point to a market that is both concentrated and evolving. Long-established names continue to account for substantial sales, while artists such as Mehretu and Emin are gaining ground, suggesting that the hierarchy of the women’s prints market is not necessarily fixed. The market, though, remains firmly anchored to 20 th- and 21 st- century production.

What publishers see before works reach auction

Auction results tell only part of the story. The primary market for prints and editions begins with artists, publishers, and printers, whose decisions about edition size, release prices, and production can shape the market long before works reach the auction block.

Conner Williams , head of prints and multiples at Artnet Auctions , notes that, “in recent years, women artists working in print have, to far less fanfare than public auction, produced editions made available directly for purchase through various print-publishers and at prices that would be noteworthy if only public. Julie Mehretu, Elizabeth Peyton , Cecily Brown , and Dana Schutz , to name a few, have collaborated with leading international publishers including BORCH Editions , Gemini G.E.L. , and Two Palms , to regularly sell their prints at prices exceeding $100,000. In many cases, these new releases outperform those of their contemporary male counterparts. Because sales in this segment of the market are often private and less transparent than public auctions, these achievements are not widely known, leaving many collectors unaware of the extraordinary demand and value these artists have generated through printmaking.”

The publishers’ perspectives can help illuminate a dimension that auction data alone cannot capture: whether interest in women artists is broadening among collectors, how publishers approach pricing, and whether strong demand at release translates into sustained secondary-market performance.

Elizabeth Peyton, Kiss (Jackson + Ally, Bradley + Stephanie, A Star is Born) #1 , 2019. Monotype on Twinrocker handmade paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions

A market still taking shape

The growing visibility of women artists in printmaking is also reflected in Artnet Auctions’ current “Premier Prints & Multiples” sale, which includes works by Julie Mehretu, Elizabeth Peyton, Vija Celmins, Mickalene Thomas, Helen Frankenthaler, Beatriz Milhazes , and Katherine Bernhardt . Spanning generations and approaches to the medium, the works offer a snapshot of the breadth of contemporary collecting of women artists in the medium.

Ultimately, the question may not be whether women artists are having a moment in prints. Museum acquisitions, institutional programming, fairs, and the auction data all point to meaningful activity. The harder question is how broadly that momentum is being felt, and whether increased visibility is translating into lasting market value across generations of women artists.

The data suggests that the relationship between gender and auction performance is more nuanced in prints and multiples than a single price-gap figure might imply.

For now, the results offer a reason to look beyond headline prices, and to ask not only which women artists are selling, but how the market for their work is evolving.

title_original: Harvesting the Future: Ibrahim Mahama Reimagines Africa’s Cultural Possibilities
editorial_title_zh: 收获未来：Ibrahim Mahama 重新想象非洲的文化可能性

article_text:
At Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain in Paris, Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama’s ‘The Harvest Season’ brings together nine artists and collectives to explore colonial histories, collective memory and the possibilities of cultural transformation.

What can the unfinished ambitions of the past teach us about the future? In ‘The Harvest Season’, Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama transforms Fondation Cartier into a space for artistic exchange, historical reflection and collective imagination.

Marking Mahama’s first major exhibition in Paris, the presentation brings together monumental installations, archival materials and site-specific works alongside contributions from nine artists and collectives. Drawing on Ghana’s colonial and postcolonial histories, Mahama examines the circulation of goods, industrial heritage and the relationship between labour, memory and power.

The exhibition extends his work beyond individual artistic production, reflecting the collaborative ethos of the cultural institutions he has established in Tamale, northern Ghana. Contributors include James Barnor, Dorothy Akpene Amenuke, Gideon Appah, Zohra Opoku and the Cercle d’Art des Travailleurs de Plantation Congolaise, whose practices engage with photography, textiles, architecture and collective histories.

Through these interconnected perspectives, ‘The Harvest Season’ revisits the political and cultural aspirations of African independence movements, questioning how unrealised possibilities might inform contemporary futures. Rather than treating history as a closed chapter, Mahama positions artistic practice as a means of recovering knowledge, sustaining cultural exchange and imagining alternative forms of collective life.

This exhibition will be on view at Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain in Paris from 22 October 2026 until 28 February 2027.

article_text:
BAFTA has a new chair.

UKTV commissioning boss Hilary Rosen will succeed Sara Putt at the UK awards body after Putt’s three-year term runs down.

Rosen has been Deputy Chair for the past year and will be succeeded in that role by Ade Rawcliffe and Andrew Miller.

Rosen is a well-regarded TV commissioner who has risen up the ranks at BBC Studios-owned UKTV to become Director of Commissioning, leading its slate of original scripted and unscripted content like Mark Gatiss’ Bookish and Mitford Sisters drama Outrageous.

Rosen said: “I have long been passionate about everything BAFTA does to promote the screen arts and champion talent across the screen industries, so it is a great privilege to take on the role of BAFTA Chair. I am delighted to be able to do this alongside our newly appointed committee chairs.”

Watch on Deadline

Those new chairs are Charu Desodt and Caroline Levy, who will chair BAFTA’s Games and Television Committees, while Nahrein Kemp will take up the role of LIT Committee Chair. Additionally, Shrina Shah, Chair of the Governance and Appointments committee will join the BAFTA Board of Trustees.

BAFTA holds TV and film awards each year plus runs training programs and events.

Sea of crimson: vivid ‘red beach’ transforms China’s wetlands and marshes – in pictures

A striking transformation takes place along the coast of Qinqdao in autumn, when a native seepweed turns a brilliant shade of red.

The ‘red beach’ phenemon can be seen in the salt marshes and wetlands on the coast of China’s Shandong province, where the Suaeda glauca plant matures and absorbs water, changing it from green to crimson between September and November

Natürlich hatte Picasso problematische Eigenschaften, als Künstler war er jedoch so erfindungsreich wie kaum ein anderer. Hier erzählt die Malerin Chunqing Huang, warum sie die "Les Demoiselles d’Avignon" noch immer faszinieren

Ich kannte Picassos "Demoiselles" natürlich von Abbildungen. Im Original habe ich es erst im vergangenen März betrachten können, auf einer Reise nach New York anlässlich einer Gruppenausstellung, an der ich beteiligt war. Das 2,30 Meter breite Original im MoMA zu sehen, ist etwas ganz Besonderes. Ein Gänsehautmoment…

Through roughly 50 artworks dating from the 1970s to the present, the exhibition explores the tantalizing intrigue of telenovelas, whose appeal transcends class, language, and geography across the Americas. Rather than dismiss melodrama as frivolous, the show’s curator, Aimé Iglesias Lukin, considers the genre’s power to unsettle seemingly calcified social and political values. The show also includes a commission by Mexican artist, performer, and educator Pablo Helguera, who’s mined the medium as a site of scholarship through his ongoing project Instituto de la Telenovela , begun in 2002. Through March 27, 2027, at 680 Park Avenue"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Miguel-Calderon-Eden-is-a-Magic-World-2011.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Image Credit: Courtesy Americas Society", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "“Incendiaries” at 80WSE Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy Fales Library and Special Collections, New York University Libraries In November 1970, Faith Ringgold, Jean Toche, and Jon Hendricks, soon to be known as the Judson Three, gathered more than 150 artists at Judson Memorial Church in New York City for “The People’s Flag Show,” a riotous, weeklong expedition to the limits of creative expression. The exhibition’s flyer called on artists to test the “repressive laws governing so-called flag desecration,” and test them they did. Among the works on view was an iteration of Yvonne Rainer’s signature dance Trio A , performed by dancers wearing American flags tied like bibs around their necks. Police raided the exhibition, and its organizers were convicted of violating New York’s flag desecration law. “We have been convicted, but in fact it is this nation and these courts who are guilty,” they declared in a statement following the ruling, which was later overturned. The exhibition was organized in solidarity with Stephen Radich, a New York art dealer whose conviction for exhibiting works that incorporated the American flag in protest of the Vietnam War brought his case before the US Supreme Court. Curated by Howie Chen with Jon Huron, “Incendiaries” arrives at New York University’s 80WSE Gallery as a kind of cultural stress test, pressing against the same social limits the Judson Three challenged more than half a century ago—and finding them as rigid as ever. In the intervening decades, a rising tide of nationalism has swept through the arts, narrowing the space for political dissent. Perseverance, however, is the point. Drawing extensively from the Judson Memorial Church Archive, including rare photographs and video documentation, “Incendiaries” traces a continuum of social activism carried forward by contemporary artists. Through January 16, 2027, at 80 Washington Square East"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/flag-show.png?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Image Credit: Courtesy Fales Library and Special Collections, New York University Libraries", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "“Locating Girlhood: Place and Identity in Early American ‘Schoolgirl’ Art” at the American Folk Art Museum Image Credit: Courtesy American Folk Art Museum This show compellingly suggests that American landscape art truly begins not with the Hudson River School’s Romantic vistas or the god-defying expanses that would eventually give way to abstraction, but with young women—including free and enslaved women of color—who rendered this nascent frontier in needle and thread. Caroline Culp, curator of American art at the Chrysler Museum of Art in Norfolk and co-organizer of the American Folk Art Museum exhibition, has assembled nearly 100 objects dating from the colonial period through the nation’s founding.
