article_text:
You’d be forgiven for thinking New York’s fall art calendar begins and ends with the museum spotlight. From the Whitney Museum’s Roy Lichtenstein retrospective to a Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock blockbuster at the Met, ’tis the season of mid-century heavyweights. But for those who’ve made the rounds—or simply like their art with a party—compelling encounters abound in group shows across the city.

Some delve into lesser-known chapters of New York art history; others bring serious scholarship to overlooked art forms. Several institutions are marking major anniversaries in business (no small feat in Manhattan) with exhibitions drawn from the collections that have sustained their programs over the years.

Read on for a decidedly non-exhaustive list of group shows to catch around the city during Art Week NYC , a four-day festival of art events taking place across the city that is being organized by ARTnews , Art in America , and Artforum .

“Telenovela” at Americas Society Image Credit: Courtesy Americas Society In honor of the soapiest of television traditions, bring your lover, their lover, a secret love child, a long-lost twin engaged in identity fraud—or triplet (por que no?)—to “Telenovela” at the Americas Society. Through roughly 50 artworks dating from the 1970s to the present, the exhibition explores the tantalizing intrigue of telenovelas, whose appeal transcends class, language, and geography across the Americas. Rather than dismiss melodrama as frivolous, the show’s curator, Aimé Iglesias Lukin, considers the genre’s power to unsettle seemingly calcified social and political values. The show also includes a commission by Mexican artist, performer, and educator Pablo Helguera, who’s mined the medium as a site of scholarship through his ongoing project Instituto de la Telenovela , begun in 2002. Through March 27, 2027, at 680 Park Avenue

“Incendiaries” at 80WSE Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy Fales Library and Special Collections, New York University Libraries In November 1970, Faith Ringgold, Jean Toche, and Jon Hendricks, soon to be known as the Judson Three, gathered more than 150 artists at Judson Memorial Church in New York City for “The People’s Flag Show,” a riotous, weeklong expedition to the limits of creative expression. The exhibition’s flyer called on artists to test the “repressive laws governing so-called flag desecration,” and test them they did. Among the works on view was an iteration of Yvonne Rainer’s signature dance Trio A , performed by dancers wearing American flags tied like bibs around their necks. Police raided the exhibition, and its organizers were convicted of violating New York’s flag desecration law. “We have been convicted, but in fact it is this nation and these courts who are guilty,” they declared in a statement following the ruling, which was later overturned. The exhibition was organized in solidarity with Stephen Radich, a New York art dealer whose conviction for exhibiting works that incorporated the American flag in protest of the Vietnam War brought his case before the US Supreme Court. Curated by Howie Chen with Jon Huron, “Incendiaries” arrives at New York University’s 80WSE Gallery as a kind of cultural stress test, pressing against the same social limits the Judson Three challenged more than half a century ago—and finding them as rigid as ever. In the intervening decades, a rising tide of nationalism has swept through the arts, narrowing the space for political dissent. Perseverance, however, is the point. Drawing extensively from the Judson Memorial Church Archive, including rare photographs and video documentation, “Incendiaries” traces a continuum of social activism carried forward by contemporary artists. Through January 16, 2027, at 80 Washington Square East

“Locating Girlhood: Place and Identity in Early American ‘Schoolgirl’ Art” at the American Folk Art Museum Image Credit: Courtesy American Folk Art Museum This show compellingly suggests that American landscape art truly begins not with the Hudson River School’s Romantic vistas or the god-defying expanses that would eventually give way to abstraction, but with young women—including free and enslaved women of color—who rendered this nascent frontier in needle and thread. Caroline Culp, curator of American art at the Chrysler Museum of Art in Norfolk and co-organizer of the American Folk Art Museum exhibition, has assembled nearly 100 objects dating from the colonial period through the nation’s founding. These include the kinds of ornamental works trivialized as women’s work: needlework pictures, watercolor studies, painted furniture, among more mediums. The show was organized with the sesquicentennial in mind, but presents a welcome counterpoint to the prevailing triumphalism, which argues art as a vehicle of national might. Through February 28, 2027, at 2 Lincoln Square.

“Buddha and Shiva, Lotus and Dragon: Celebrating 70 Years of Asia Society and the Rockefeller Legacy” at Asia Society Image Credit: Asia Society, New York: Mr. and Mrs. John D. Rockefeller 3rd Collection, 1979.38 The Asia Society is marking 70 years in Manhattan with an exhibition of 70 devotional sculptures and ceramics from its renowned Rockefeller collection. The selection offers a spectacular introduction to a trove spanning two millennia of Asian art, from an 11th-century bronze figure of the Hindu goddess Parvati to a mid-17th-century Japanese tea-leaf jar delicately painted with black myna birds and a strikingly embossed silver stem cup from China, dated to the late 7th or early 8th century. Organized by Asia Society and the American Federation of Arts, the exhibition was first presented in 2020 under the direction of Adriana Proser, then the Asia Society Museum’s senior curator. It has now returned in an expanded iteration, curated by assistant curator Xiaohan Du, to commemorate the museum’s founding in 1956 by John D. Rockefeller III, grandson of the Standard Oil magnate. Rockefeller and his wife, Blanchette Hooker Rockefeller, assembled most of the collection between the 1950s and ’70s and donated it to Asia Society in 1979. Look out for recent additions by two of their children, Sandra Ferry Rockefeller and Hope Aldrich, who carry the family’s collecting legacy into the present. Through January 3, 2027 , at 725 Park Avenue.

“Art of Manga” at Brooklyn Museum Image Credit: Courtesy Brooklyn Museum As any millennial cosplayer in the West can attest, over the past decade manga has moved from niche interest to pop-culture powerhouse. Making its East Coast debut at the Brooklyn Museum, “The Art of Manga” marks another milestone in that ascent: an institutional survey of the Japanese comics form that attracted more than 176,000 visitors in a previous iteration at the de Young museum in San Francisco. The exhibition features more than 600 original drawings by some of the medium’s biggest names, including Takahashi Rumiko ( Inuyasha ), Oda Eiichiro ( One Piece ), and Araki Hirohiko ( JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure ). Tracing manga’s historical roots through its contemporary iterations, the show considers how the form reflects and interrogates social conventions around gender, sexuality, and class disparity. Through January 31, 2027, at 200 Eastern Parkway.

“Siena: The Art of Bronze, 1450–1500” at the Frick Collection Image Credit: © The Frick Collection In typical accounts of the Italian Renaissance, Florence tends to hog the spotlight, with Milan and Venice not far behind. “Siena: The Art of Bronze, 1450–1500” makes a case for the Tuscan city—about 30 miles south of Florence—as a center of artistic ingenuity in its own right. Organized by Frick associate curator Giulio Dalvit, the exhibition brings together works by influential sculptors including Donatello, Vecchietta, and Francesco di Giorgio, reconsidering their bronzes against a pivotal chapter in the history of Sienese workshops. Here, technical innovation is cast in the same mold as the political and social forces that forged Renaissance art. Through January 18, 2027, at 1 East 70th Street.

“Fields of Color X” at Yares Art Image Credit: Courtesy Yares Art. Perhaps a stop in the midcentury is unavoidable, since this is New York City, after all. “Fields of Color X” brings together key works by leading painters of the Color Field movement, including Helen Frankenthaler, Kenneth Noland, Adolph Gottlieb, and Jules Olitski, to illuminate their professional and personal relationships. It’s an admirable undertaking: When the subject is one of the most celebrated movements in art history, what new insights can emerge from the technical and conceptual interplay of these painting? Whatever the answer, an afternoon in the company of these blushing, blooming canvases is its own reward. Through January 2027 , at 745 5th Avenue.

“All That Before Us” at Ruiz-Healy Art Image Credit: Courtesy Ruiz-Healy Art In “All That Before Us,” Jennifer Ling Datchuk and Consuelo Jimenez Underwood challenge a twofold hierarchy: one that relegates ceramics, textiles, and sculptural assemblage to the realm of craft, and the patriarchal order that has devalued both women’s labor and the materials associated with it. Datchuk’s porcelain works reckon with domestic labor and femininity, while two vessels inspired by Song dynasty ceramics are home to the chinoiserie motifs that recur in her visual vocabulary, alongside fertility figurines, extraterrestrials, pregnancy tests, and hair accessories. Jimenez Underwood, meanwhile, reimagines the Mesoamerican rebozo as a functional record of cultural memory, migration, and identity. Together, their works collapse the distance between ancestral traditions and modern politics. Through November 27, 2026, at 74 East 79th Street.

editorial_title_zh: 全员去巴黎！2026年巴黎巴塞尔艺术展完整指南
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这场超级秋季艺博会即将开幕，超过210家国际画廊齐聚大皇宫。以下是关于各个展区和特别项目的所有必知信息，助您轻松逛展……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "正当伦敦仍处于弗里兹周（Frieze Week）的中心之际，艺术界正准备横渡英吉利海峡，齐聚巴黎。2026年巴黎巴塞尔艺术展将于10月23日至25日（其中10月21日和22日为预展日）重返大皇宫，迎来2026年展会，进一步巩固其在国际艺术日历中最重要的活动之一的地位。卡里姆·克里帕（Karim Crippa）首次出任展会总监，此前他曾担任巴黎巴塞尔艺术展的传讯总监及巴黎巴塞尔艺术展全球高级编辑。“我将尽一切努力推动这一非凡的艺博会不断向前发展，并作为巴黎这座城市、我们的参展商、我们的合作伙伴以及巴黎巴塞尔艺术展使命的坚定支持者，”他透露道。在他的带领下，共有211家画廊参展，来自41个国家和地区，展出项目交织了现代与当代艺术巨匠、全新声音以及策展项目。从核心展区到与艺术家和策展人的对话，以下是了解展会、锁定最有趣活动并规划参观行程所需掌握的一切。", "links": [{"text": "Karim Crippa", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/mercato/cambio-ai-vertici-karim-crippa-e-il-nuovo-direttore-di-art-basel-paris/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "日期与地点：2026年巴黎巴塞尔艺术展何时举办", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "巴黎巴塞尔艺术展将于2026年10月23日至25日在温斯顿·丘吉尔大道（Avenue Winston Churchill）的大皇宫举行。预展日定于10月21日星期三和10月22日星期四，仅限受邀者参加，并为收藏家和行业专业人士设专属场次。艺博会将于10月23日星期五、24日星期六和25日星期日对公众开放，时间为11点至19点。对于在弗里兹艺博会之后从伦敦赶来的观众而言，日程表在两项活动之间提供了一种近乎自然的过渡，在短短几天内集中了艺术品市场秋季赛季的重要部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/01_HiRes-1024x670.jpg", "alt": "art basel paris 2026", "caption": "Galleries.Gianni Manhattan Sebastian Jefford, Clock test (72 years old), Clock test (79 years old), 2025 Courtesy the artist, Kunstverein Bielefeld, GIANNI MANHATTAN, Vienna and Galerie Noah Klink, Berlin", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "2026年展会数字：总计211家画廊", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "共有211家画廊参展，来自41个国家和地区。其中，183家在主展区Galeries参展，16家在Emergence参展，12家在Premise参展。32家画廊首次参加巴黎巴塞尔艺术展，而超过170家画廊在历届展会后再度回归。法国本土画廊的参与度依然核心，有64家总部位于法国的画廊。艺博会的结构将专注于国际画廊的主展区与两个更有针对性的板块相结合，即Emergence和Premise，分别旨在支持新锐探索和重读艺术史的项目。除此之外，还有特别活动、对话项目以及公共空间中的艺术介入。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Kandinsky_1922_HiRes-1024x702.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Art Basel Paris 2026. article_text:
Mentre Londra è ancora al centro della settimana di Frieze, il mondo dell’arte si prepara ad attraversare la Manica e a ritrovarsi a Parigi. Dal 23 al 25 ottobre, con le preview del 21 e 22 ottobre 2026, Art Basel Paris torna al Grand Palais per la sua edizione 2026, consolidando il proprio ruolo tra gli appuntamenti più importanti del calendario internazionale. Per la prima volta è Karim Crippa a dirigerla, prima Direttore della Comunicazione di Art Basel Paris e Senior Editor Worldwide di Art Basel. «Farò tutto il possibile per far progredire questa fiera eccezionale e rimarrò un instancabile sostenitore della città di Parigi, dei nostri espositori, dei nostri partner e della missione di Art Basel», ha rivelato. 211 sotto la sua guida, provengono da 41 Paesi e territori, con un programma che intreccia grandi nomi dell’arte moderna e contemporanea, nuove voci e progetti curatoriali. Dalle sezioni principali agli incontri con artisti e curatori, ecco tutto quello che bisogna sapere per orientarsi nella fiera, individuare gli appuntamenti più interessanti e organizzare la visita.

Date e location: quando si svolge Art Basel Paris 2026

Art Basel Paris si terrà al Grand Palais, su Avenue Winston Churchill, dal 23 al 25 ottobre 2026. Le giornate di preview sono previste per mercoledì 21 e giovedì 22 ottobre, con accesso solo su invito e sessioni dedicate ai collezionisti e agli operatori del settore. La fiera sarà aperta al pubblico venerdì 23, sabato 24 e domenica 25 ottobre, dalle 11 alle 19. Per chi arriva da Londra dopo Frieze, il calendario offre un passaggio quasi naturale tra i due appuntamenti, concentrando in pochi giorni una parte importante della stagione autunnale del mercato dell’arte.

I numeri dell’edizione 2026: 211 gallerie totali

Sono 211 le gallerie partecipanti, provenienti da 41 Paesi e territori. Di queste, 183 espongono nella sezione principale Galeries, 16 in Emergence e 12 in Premise. Trentadue gallerie partecipano per la prima volta ad Art Basel Paris, mentre oltre 170 tornano dopo le edizioni precedenti. La presenza francese resta centrale, con 64 gallerie con sede in Francia. La struttura della fiera combina una sezione principale dedicata alle gallerie internazionali con due settori più mirati, Emergence e Premise, pensati rispettivamente per le ricerche emergenti e per progetti che rileggono la storia dell’arte. A questi si aggiungono iniziative speciali, un programma di incontri e interventi artistici nello spazio pubblico.

Galeries: 183 gallerie, tra grandi nomi e debutti da seguire

È il settore principale della fiera, con un programma che attraversa modernismo, dopoguerra e contemporaneo. Accanto ai giganti – tutti presenti – come Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, White Cube e Thaddaeus Ropac, l’edizione 2026 dà particolare rilievo ai nuovi ingressi: 11 gallerie partecipano per la prima volta al settore, mentre sei espositori provenienti da Emergence entrano nella sezione principale, tra cui Petrine e The Pill. Tra i progetti da cercare, Larkin Erdmann presenta due opere emblematiche di Marcel Duchamp e Man Ray, L.H.O.O.Q. e Violon d’Ingres , e riporta sul mercato per la prima volta dopo quasi mezzo secolo un dipinto di On Kawara del 1977. Da Pilar Corrias, Christina Quarles presenta invece un monumentale trittico che cambierà configurazione nel corso della fiera, trasformando lo stand in un’installazione in evoluzione. Carlos/Ishikawa presenta nuovi dipinti di Moka Lee, che indagano il ritratto nell’era delle immagini digitali. Un altro dato significativo è il numero di collaborazioni tra gallerie: dodici stand condivisi da 24 realtà, con progetti che mettono in dialogo artisti, generazioni e pratiche differenti. È un formato che supera la tradizionale logica della presentazione individuale e offre letture trasversali di temi come identità, memoria, corpo e storia.

Le gallerie italiane (o con sede in Italia) da incontrare tra le sezioni di Art Basel Paris 2026

Diversi gli espositori italiani di Art Basel Paris 2026, o con almeno una sede nel Paese. Ne menzioniamo alcuni: n ella sezione principale Galeries troviamo Alfonso Artiaco (Napoli), Cardi Gallery (Milano), Emanuela Campoli (Milano e Parigi), Fanta-MLN (Milano), Galleria Continua (San Gimignano e altre sedi internazionali ), Galleria Raffaella Cortese (Milano), Gió Marconi (Milano), Galleria Franco Noero (Torino), kaufmann repetto (Milano e New York), Laveronica arte contemporanea (Modica), Massimodecarlo (Milano e altre sedi in giro per il monso ), P420 (Bologna) e Tornabuoni Art, presente in diverse città . Si aggiungono Consonni Radziszewski, con una sede a Milano, e le gallerie internazionali Gagosian e Gladstone Gallery, entrambe presenti anche a Roma, Thaddaeus Ropac a Milano, Victoria Miro a Venezia, ancora ermes ermes nella sezione Emergence.

Emergence: 16 artisti e nuove ricerche internazionali

Quindi, ecco le altre categorie. Collocata sui balconi della navata centrale del Grand Palais, Emergence riunisce 16 presentazioni personali dedicate ad artisti emergenti. Dodici gallerie partecipano per la prima volta alla sezione, con progetti che spaziano dall’installazione alla pittura, dalla scultura ai linguaggi multimediali. Molte opere sono state concepite o prodotte appositamente per la fiera. Tra i nomi da segnare c’è Angharad Williams, presentata dalla galleria KIN con cinque grandi dipinti a olio raffiguranti banchi di trote e un nuovo video in prima persona che mette in discussione il confine tra desiderio e consumo. Lorenza Longhi, da Oskar Weiss, porta invece un progetto che combina pittura, stampa serigrafica e PVC, con riferimenti alla cultura pop e alla sorveglianza. Haneyl Choi, presentata da P21, esplora la trasformazione e l’instabilità del corpo attraverso quattro sculture in tecnica mista. La sezione riflette una geografia ampia, con gallerie provenienti da Europa, Medio Oriente, Asia e Americhe. Tra le altre presentazioni da tenere d’occhio figurano le fotografie analogiche e gli oggetti elettroplaccati di Nat Faulkner, da Brunette Coleman, realizzati anche attraverso pellicole radiografiche riciclate, e i dipinti su seta e lacca di Thảo Nguyên Phan, da ROH, che intrecciano architettura postcoloniale e astrazione vietnamita.

Premise: le storie dell’arte da rileggere

Con 12 progetti, nove dei quali presentati da gallerie al loro debutto ad Art Basel Paris, Premise è la sezione più orientata alla ricerca storico-artistica. Nel 2026 si trasferisce nel più ampio Salon Seine, uno spazio che consente di accogliere tre progetti in più rispetto all’edizione precedente. Tra i punti di maggiore interesse, Eric Mouchet dedica una presentazione a Robert Michel e al suo periodo dadaista a Weimar, tra il 1919 e il 1921. Pavec espone tre grandi tele della serie Sources di Jacqueline Lamba, realizzate tra il 1960 e il 1980 e provenienti direttamente dall’eredità dell’artista. Galerie Zlotowski propone invece opere di Vera Molnár datate tra il 1947 e il 1956, che permettono di ripercorrere le premesse concettuali della sua successiva ricerca algoritmica. Tra i debutti spicca anche Amanda Wilkinson Gallery con i Black Paintings di Derek Jarman, realizzati tra il 1989 e il 1991: superfici scure attraversate da oggetti, croci e specchi, in una riflessione su memoria, alchimia e visibilità durante gli anni dell’AIDS. La galleria nigeriana kó riunisce invece opere di Uche Okeke, Obiora Udechukwu ed El Anatsui, ricostruendo il percorso della Nsukka School e il suo rapporto con le tradizioni visive igbo. Una sezione che invita a guardare al passato non come a un repertorio immobile, ma come a una storia ancora aperta.

Oh La La!: miti, leggende e immaginari contemporanei tra gli stand di Art Basel Paris 2026

Tra i progetti speciali dell’edizione 2026, ad Art Basel Paris, figura Oh La La! , con la direzione artistica dell’attrice francese Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu – nota anche per il suo ruolo di Sylvie Grateau nella serie Emily in Paris . Il tema scelto è Myths and Legends : non soltanto miti classici e racconti fondativi, ma anche mitologie personali, memoria ancestrale, metamorfosi, natura e immaginari contemporanei. Il progetto coinvolge le gallerie partecipanti attraverso nuove presentazioni e riallestimenti dei propri stand, concentrati nelle giornate di venerdì e sabato. Tra gli artisti annunciati figurano Nina Childress, Ossip Zadkine, Portia Zvavahera e Philippe Mayaux. Più che una sezione autonoma, Oh La La! funziona come un filo tematico che attraversa la fiera, invitando a osservare alcune opere attraverso una chiave di lettura comune.

Conversations: gli incontri da segnare in agenda

Per l’edizione 2026 di Art Basel Paris, il programma Conversations si sposta nell’Auditorium del Grand Palais, con incontri dedicati al rapporto tra arte, istituzioni, collezionismo e società. Gli appuntamenti sono gratuiti e riuniscono artisti, curatori, direttori museali e protagonisti della cultura internazionale. Tra i dialoghi in programma figurano quello tra Simone Fattal e Hans Ulrich Obrist e l’incontro dedicato al rapporto tra artista e collezionista con Eva Jospin e Laurent Dumas. Il direttore del Centre Pompidou Laurent Le Bon dialogherà con la giornalista Claire Chazal sul futuro dell’istituzione. Sono previsti anche approfondimenti con Ibrahim Mahama e Zanele Muholi, dedicati rispettivamente al ruolo delle istituzioni culturali e alla fotografia come strumento per contrastare la cancellazione delle storie marginalizzate. Per chi vuole andare oltre la visita degli stand, Conversations offre un’occasione per approfondire alcune delle questioni centrali del dibattito artistico contemporaneo. Il programma completo, con giorni e orari, è consultabile sul sito ufficiale della fiera.

Il Public Program: le opere fuori dal Grand Palais

Il programma pubblico estende la presenza di Art Basel Paris 2026 oltre gli spazi espositivi, con interventi artistici collocati in alcuni luoghi della città. Sculture e installazioni trasformano spazi pubblici e istituzionali in un percorso parallelo, accessibile anche a chi non visita la fiera. Tra i progetti annunciati figurano opere di Tracey Emin al Parvis des Droits de l’Homme, l’installazione video Küba di Kutluğ Ataman alla Chapelle des Petits-Augustins des Beaux-Arts de Paris e le sculture tessili di Cosima von Bonin al Petit Palais. A Place Clemenceau sarà presentata LOVE Wall di Robert Indiana, mentre lungo Avenue Winston Churchill sono previsti interventi di artisti come Alicja Kwade, Carmen Herrera, Niki de Saint Phalle e Yinka Shonibare. Il Public Program è parte integrante della manifestazione e consente di incontrare alcune delle ricerche artistiche presentate in un contesto diverso da quello commerciale degli stand. Date e sedi dei singoli interventi sono da verificare nel programma ufficiale.

article_text:
George Osborne, the former British chancellor who now chairs the British Museum , played a personal role in securing a reported £5 million ($6.6 million) sponsorship from billionaire hedge fund manager Igor Tulchinsky, according to internal emails obtained by the campaign group Culture Unstained.

The correspondence, first reported by in the Art Journal , shows that Osborne introduced Tulchinsky to the museum and gave the go-ahead for sponsorship negotiations less than 90 minutes after receiving a due diligence report that included a section on potential concerns about the donor. What those concerns were remains a mystery, since the museum blacked out that part of the report before releasing it under Britain’s Freedom of Information Act.

Tulchinsky, who founded the investment firm WorldQuant, has become a major backer of the British Museum’s exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry . But his reported connections to Israeli military technology companies and his alleged financial support for a community center in an Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank have attracted criticism from some left wing campaigners.

The newly released emails offer a look at how his relationship with the museum came together.

In October 2025, Charlotte Appleyard, the museum’s director of development, reportedly sent Osborne an assessment of the prospective donor and asked whether she could move ahead with discussions. Osborne replied within an hour and a half, saying he was “happy to proceed.”

By November 24, the deal was apparently done. Appleyard emailed Osborne to say Tulchinsky had agreed to sponsor the exhibition and thanked him for making the introduction.

The emails establish Osborne’s involvement in arranging the sponsorship, but according to the Art Journal , they don’t show whether the museum’s other trustees were told about the due diligence findings. Nor do they establish that the museum broke any of its own rules in accepting the money.

The controversy centers in part on Tulchinsky’s reported support for a community center in Efrat, an Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank. Israeli settlements there are considered illegal under international law, though Israel disputes that position.

On October 13, British culture minister Ian Murray told Parliament that the government hadn’t investigated reports of Tulchinsky’s involvement with the Efrat project. He said responsibility for accepting donations rests with the museum’s trustees, who are expected to follow the institution’s sponsorship policies.

Meanwhile, Tulchinsky has received recognition for his generosity. The museum has named a room in its members facilities after him, featured him in exhibition publicity, and displayed a portrait of him painted by Jonathan Yeo.

He’s also listed as honorary chair of the museum’s Red Ball fundraiser, scheduled for Saturday. The event, held in the museum’s Great Court, will feature artistic direction by Es Devlin and a performance by Wyclef Jean.

Culture Unstained, the activist group which obtained the emails, argues that the museum needs to rethink how it evaluates wealthy donors, particularly when the same person helping bring in the money is also responsible for overseeing the institution.

“The Museum’s approach to ethical sponsorship needs a complete overhaul,” a spokesperson for the group told the Art Journal .

The British Museum is hardly new to arguments over where its money comes from. Its $66 million, 10-year partnership with oil giant BP has drawn protests from political and environmental activists, while earlier sponsorship arrangements with tobacco companies have also faced criticism .

“The Museum is grateful for the substantial gift and support provided by Igor Tulchinsky, which helped make the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition possible,” a spokesperson told ARTnews via email. “The Museum considers all sponsorship opportunities in line with our published policy.”

article_text:
LALIQUE and Fang Lijun / Yawning Man 2.0 / Nov 2 – 8, 2026 /

Tournament Village / Victoria Park / Causeway Bay / Hong Kong /

laliquehk.com

Renowned French crystal brand LALIQUE has collaborated with Chinese contemporary artist Fang Lijun to present Yawning Man 2.0 , a crystal artwork making its Hong Kong debut during this year’s Hong Kong Tennis Open. Also on display at the Tournament Village is a distinctive eco-friendly artwork 2025-2026 by Fang Lijun, reflecting the importance and future in the cross-disciplinary fusion of sports and art.

After a decade of exploration and refinement, Yawning Man 2.0 brings together Fang Lijun’s artistic vision and LALIQUE’s century-old savoir-faire of crystal. Transcending the boundaries of traditional artistic media, Fang reimagines his iconic painting Series 2, (No. 2) , combining its signature bald, yawning figure with the luminous clarity of crystal.

The Yawning Man 2.0 crystal artworks are crafted entirely by hand at the LALIQUE workshops in Alsace, France. Using the precise traditional lost-wax casting technique, LALIQUE’s artisans translate the distinctive contours of Fang’s bald figure into a radiant, three-dimensional crystal form. From the original sculpture, a silicone mould is created and filled with molten wax to form a precise wax model, which is then encased in plaster. Heated until the wax flows away, the mould preserves every contour of the sculpture before two crystal colours are poured within. Blending with subtle grace, the hues flow differently in each creation, embracing every detail and rendering each piece entirely unique. Once cooled, the single-use plaster mould is gently broken to reveal the finished crystal work.
